text: Course 11 already made the case that a DR plan nobody has run is a hypothesis. The part it didn't fully cover is who, or what, should actually execute that plan when a disaster is real. The honest answer at enterprise scale is: not a person who just got paged awake at three in the morning, staring at a runbook they haven't touched in months, deciding under pressure whether this is really the moment to pull the trigger.

Three things make a human the weak link here. Detection is slow — paging, waking up, and reading through a runbook burns minutes that a health check doesn't need. Execution is error-prone — fatigue and adrenaline are exactly the conditions where steps get skipped or run out of order. And the runbook itself is often stale, because a procedure nobody has executed since it was written is, as course 11 put it, a guess dressed up as a plan.

Automated failover fixes the detection half: health checks across multiple independent signals — not one flaky probe — watch for sustained failure and rising error-budget burn, and the system triggers failover itself once several checks agree, specifically to avoid failing over on a transient blip that would have resolved on its own.

Runbook-as-code fixes the execution half. Instead of a wiki page a human interprets under pressure, the actual recovery procedure is executable code: promote the standby data store, repoint DNS, scale up the DR region to full capacity, verify the dependencies that Lesson 14's graph says have to come up in the right order, then page on-call with a status, not a request for action. That code runs the same way every time, drills included, which is exactly what keeps it from going stale the way an unexecuted runbook does.

None of this removes humans from DR entirely — slower tiers can still route through a human approval step, and every automated path needs a kill switch. But for the tier with a seconds-level RTO, no human reaction time qualifies, and automation is the only thing that does. The real test of whether any of this actually works, automated or not, is the next lesson: running it for real, at production scale.
